questions.question: By the California ISO's own reported total interchange, what share of its demand was met by net imports in August 2026, in percent?
questions.answer: By CAISO's own EIA-reported total interchange, net imports met 8.29% of its demand in August 2026 (ba_supply_monthly, variable net_import_total_interchange_share_pct, entity eia930:CISO, monthly value for the 31 August days, all days held, derived table). The net import was 2,101,671 MWh against demand of 25,338,610 MWh. The month is the August calendar month, labelled at 2026-08-01T00:00Z. A positive value means the neighbours supplied CAISO. As a side note, the table's supply-minus-generation balance gives a higher 19.66%. The warehouse notes that CAISO's published net generation dropped from December 2025, which makes that balance read about 10 points higher than its flows.

questions.question: For ERCOT projects that reached operation in 2024, what was the median time from interconnection request to operation, in months?
questions.answer: For the 95 ERCOT projects that reached operation in 2024, the median time from interconnection request to operation was 43.5 months. The project-level table interconnection_durations gives this directly (median of months_to_operation). The yearly table interconnection_durations_summary gives the same 43.5 months (median_months, entity lbnl_durations:ercot, 2024). The middle half of projects took 28.25 to 55.75 months (25th and 75th percentiles, interconnection_durations). These figures are the ERW's derived arithmetic on Berkeley Lab's Queued Up file, and the 2024 group covers completed projects only.

# ERCOT: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) runs the power grid for most of Texas. It is a grid operator, not a utility: it owns no power plants and no power lines. It schedules the plants that others own, keeps supply equal to demand every second, and runs the wholesale market where power is bought and sold. The Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Texas Legislature oversee it. Parts of Texas, near El Paso, in the Panhandle and in the east, belong to other grids.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

ERCOT runs two markets. In the day-ahead market, buyers and sellers agree today on power for each hour of tomorrow. In the real-time market, ERCOT dispatches plants every few minutes and pays the price at that moment. Prices are set at each location on the grid (locational marginal prices), so power costs more where lines are congested. A hub, such as the Hub Average on this page, averages many locations into one price that traders use. ERCOT has no capacity market: generators are paid only for the energy they sell and some reliability services, so prices during scarce hours can rise very high, which is meant to reward being available.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/mktinfo ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

ERCOT is an island. Its grid has only a few small links to the rest of the country and to Mexico, so it cannot lean on its neighbors in an emergency, and because its power does not cross state lines in a big way, the federal regulator (FERC) does not set its market rules. It is also the energy-only market described above. Texas produces more wind electricity than any other state (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/wind/where-wind-power-is-harnessed.php) and is adding large amounts of solar and batteries, so the mix on this page changes a lot between a windy night and a sunny afternoon.

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about/profile ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/ERCO

## A short history

- **1970:** ERCOT is formed to manage reliability for the Texas grid (ERCOT, https://www.ercot.com/news/mediakit/backgrounder).
- **2010-12-01:** ERCOT starts its nodal market, with a price at each location on the grid instead of a few zones (ERCOT, https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2011/04/26/ercot_2010_financial_statements.pdf).
- **2021-02-15:** During Winter Storm Uri, ERCOT orders utilities to cut power to customers across the state because too many power plants had failed in the cold (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=46836).

Sources: https://www.ercot.com/about ; https://www.ercot.com/about/profile

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports ERCOT as balancing authority ERCO.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price.
- **Peak and off-peak:** peak hours are weekday daytime hours when demand is high; the rest are off-peak.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.
- **Interconnection queue:** the waiting list of new power plants and batteries asking to connect to the grid.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us.php

# PJM: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

PJM Interconnection runs the largest wholesale electricity market in the United States (PJM, https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/who-we-are). Its grid covers all or part of thirteen states and the District of Columbia (PJM, https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/who-we-are), from New Jersey and Pennsylvania west to Illinois and south to Virginia and North Carolina. PJM owns no power plants: it schedules the plants that its members own, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans the high-voltage transmission lines. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules.

Sources: https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm ; https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/who-we-are ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

Like the other large grids, PJM runs a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes. Prices are set at each location on the grid (locational marginal prices), so power costs more where lines are congested. PJM also pays power plants, batteries and customers who can cut their use to be available years ahead, through its capacity market (next section).

Sources: https://www.pjm.com/markets-and-operations/energy ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

The capacity auction. Each year PJM runs an auction, the Reliability Pricing Model (RPM), that buys a promise of enough generating capacity for a future delivery year (PJM, https://www.pjm.com/markets-and-operations/rpm). The result sets a price per megawatt per day that every customer's bill pays for, so a high auction price is news across the whole region. PJM also serves Northern Virginia's large and growing cluster of datacenters, which makes it a sharp example of AI's demand for power. PJM's prices are licensed to the ERW for internal use only, so this page does not show them.

Sources: https://www.pjm.com/markets-and-operations/rpm ; https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/who-we-are

## A short history

- **1927:** Three utilities in Pennsylvania and New Jersey pool their power plants; PJM grows from this pool (PJM, https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/who-we-are/pjm-history).
- **2007:** PJM's capacity market, the Reliability Pricing Model, begins with its 2007/2008 delivery year (PJM Manual 18, https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m18.pdf).
- **2022-12-24:** During Winter Storm Elliott, many power plants fail in the cold and PJM calls on emergency procedures to keep the lights on (PJM, https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2023/20230717-winter-storm-elliott-event-analysis-and-recommendation-report.pdf).

Sources: https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/who-we-are ; https://www.pjm.com/markets-and-operations/rpm

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports PJM as balancing authority PJM.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Capacity market:** a market that pays resources to be available in a future year, separate from paying for the energy they produce.
- **Reliability Pricing Model (RPM):** PJM's capacity market and its yearly auction.
- **Datacenter:** a building full of computer servers; large ones use as much power as a small city.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.pjm.com/markets-and-operations/rpm
